correctness.rationale: Explicit Rayleigh moment identities and t^-2 cycle-tail imply logarithmic truncated variance, which yields the sqrt(n log n) triangular-array central limit theorem. Renewal-clock inversion proves the current-index limit. A marked renewal theorem controls the reward of the cycle straddling t; stopped-martingale isometry makes centered rewards negligible at the nonequilibrium scale. The known exact raw second-moment coefficient is independently reconstructed by renewal Laplace transforms and checked against Horii et al. 2022 Eq. (61). Equilibrium finite-variance time change and isometry give the sqrt(t) law. All hypotheses and the L>0, beta>0 domain are explicit; 18 finite checks passed but were not used as an infinite proof.

originality.rationale: The assessed contribution is the nonequilibrium Gaussian weak law with variance coefficient half that of the already published total current variance, plus its sharp equilibrium normalization boundary. Full-text examinations found earlier equilibrium Green-Kubo, large-deviation, moment-generating and raw-variance results, but not this distribution-level comparison. Raw variance is credited, not asserted novel; generic renewal limit theorems supply proof ingredients and remain a stated priority risk.
residual_risks: Strong general-renewal theorem may imply weak Gaussian distribution without naming the physical thermal-wall model; historical priority of this synthesis is not independently certified.
The 2022 paper already gives the entire nonequilibrium raw-variance coefficient and the model: treating that quantity as new would be false.
Some older general renewal CLT sources or inaccessible writings might contain the complete two-component statement.

value.rationale: The mismatch is an experimentally meaningful warning: the coefficient inferred from raw ensemble variance overestimates typical Gaussian heat-current fluctuations by a factor of two, and equal-temperature calibration abruptly removes the logarithmic scaling. Dependence of heat reward and flight time must be handled, so it is more than an isolated numerical parameter case. Independent many-body or non-Rayleigh extensions remain unproved.
